Note: Ahura Mazda relates to Asha Vahishta as the embodiment of his own perfect truth and cosmic order (Asha), expressing the lawful structure through which reality is rightly arranged.

In the Old Avestan tradition, Spenta Mainyu is the bounteous or beneficent spirit closely associated with Ahura Mazda’s creative activity. Whether it is simply an aspect of Ahura Mazda or a more distinct hypostasis remains debated.
Ahura Mazda relates to Vohu Manah as the expression of divine intelligence and ethical consciousness, enabling humans to perceive and align with his truth.
Ahura Mazda relates to Spenta Armaiti as the principle of devoted alignment and grounding, through which his order becomes stabilized and embodied in the world.

Secondary Name: Yasna Haptanghaiti and Old Avestan Liturgy
Note: Ahura Mazda is addressed directly as the Wise Lord—the source of truth (asha), right mind, and moral order—invoked in both personal dialogue and communal worship.
In the Gathas, Ahura Mazda is addressed personally in an inquiry-driven, questioning dialogue.

In the selected Yashts, Ahura Mazda remains the supreme creator and source of order, while individual hymns praise a wider body of yazatas and inherited Iranian divine figures whose authority is ultimately situated within Mazda-worship.
Ahura Mazda legitimizes Darius’ rule by framing his victories as the triumph of truth over the Lie.
Ahura Mazda is presented as creator and source of order, whose authority underwrites the king’s role as builder and organizer of the world.
Ahura Mazda is invoked as both the source of royal authority and the standard by which the king’s justice and conduct are measured.
In XPa, Ahura Mazda is invoked as the divine source of Xerxes’ kingship and as the power by whose favor the Gate of All Nations was built.

Xerxes presents Ahura Mazda as the supreme divine authority and says that he destroyed a place where daiva were worshipped. The inscription condemns daiva worship, but it does not by itself prove exclusive monotheism.

Secondary Name: Royal Inscriptions of Artaxerxes I and II
Note: Artaxerxes I continues the conventional invocation of Ahura Mazda. In inscriptions of Artaxerxes II, Ahura Mazda is explicitly invoked together with Anāhitā and Mithra as protector of the king and his works.

Throughout the Vendidad, Ahura Mazda instructs Zarathustra in a sustained question-and-answer framework concerning sacred geography, purity, pollution, ritual practice, offenses, and resistance to demonic corruption.
In the Gathas, Angra Mainyu is the destructive orientation that emerges from choosing falsehood over truth.
In the selected Yashts, Angra Mainyu appears as the hostile power behind destructive beings and opposition to the good creation, within a more fully developed Younger Avestan cosmic conflict.
In the Vendidad, Angra Mainyu is a concrete adversary who counter-creates plagues, pollution, disease, and other corruptions against the good lands and creatures of Ahura Mazda.

Secondary Name: Yasna Haptanghaiti and Old Avestan Liturgy
Note: The Yasna Haptanghaiti explicitly praises Aša, including the formulation Aša Vahišta, as the truth and right order within which worship and communal life are properly conducted.
Aša is explicitly and repeatedly named in the Gathas as truth, right order, and the standard opposed to the Lie. The later fixed personality Aša Vahišta develops from this Old Avestan principle.
Aša Vahišta is explicitly named in the Younger Avestan hymn corpus among the Amesha Spentas and is closely associated with sacred fire in developed Zoroastrian liturgy.

The Vendidad explicitly invokes Aša Vahišta and repeatedly frames purity and right ritual as defenses of asha against pollution and the Druj; the text does not reduce Aša Vahišta to the legal code itself.

Secondary Name: Yasna Haptanghaiti and Old Avestan Liturgy
Note: The Yasna Haptanghaiti invokes Ahura Mazda’s Spenta Mainyu, his bounteous or beneficent spirit, within communal worship; it is not yet sharply presented as an independent divine personality.

Spenta Mainyu is explicitly present in the Gathas as the bounteous or beneficent spirit associated with good creation and opposed to the destructive spirit. Its precise relation to Ahura Mazda remains debated.

In the Younger Avestan hymn corpus, Spenta Mainyu is explicitly associated with the beneficent creation and contrasted with Angra Mainyu’s destructive activity, while its relationship to Ahura Mazda remains theologically layered.
The Vendidad repeatedly contrasts the good lands and creatures associated with Spenta Mainyu and Ahura Mazda with the counter-creations and pollution produced by Angra Mainyu.
Mithra is the central deity of Yasht 10, where he appears as the vigilant guardian of covenants and oaths who observes deception, punishes oath-breakers, and protects social and political order.

Secondary Name: Royal Inscriptions of Artaxerxes I and II
Note: In inscriptions of Artaxerxes II, Mithra is explicitly invoked together with Ahura Mazda and Anāhitā to protect the king and his building. This does not apply to the inscriptions of Artaxerxes I in the same bundled entry.

Secondary Name: Yasna Haptanghaiti and Old Avestan Liturgy
Note: The Yasna Haptanghaiti explicitly invokes Vohu Manah, Good Mind, as a divine principle through which worshippers align thought and action with Ahura Mazda and asha.

In the Gathas, Vohu Manah functions as the primary epistemic and ethical interface—the faculty through which Zarathustra encounters Ahura Mazda and by which humans discern and choose Asha over the Lie.

Vohu Manah is explicitly named in the Younger Avestan corpus among the Amesha Spentas and in liturgical enumerations. The developed tradition especially associates him with good purpose and the protection of cattle.

Secondary Name: Yasna Haptanghaiti and Old Avestan Liturgy
Note: The Yasna Haptanghaiti explicitly invokes Spenta Ārmaiti as holy devotion or right-mindedness within the community’s worship of Ahura Mazda.

In the Gathas, Ārmaiti functions as the ethical-existential alignment of the self with truth—a conscious choice of humble devotion through which one enters into right relation with Ahura Mazda and participates in Asha.

Spenta Ārmaiti is explicitly named in the Younger Avestan corpus among the Amesha Spentas as holy devotion or right-mindedness; her strong association with the earth is especially developed in later tradition.
Mašya and Mašyānā are the primordial human pair in later Zoroastrian cosmogony, represented as siblings who become mates and ancestors of humanity.
Harahvaitī (Harauvatiš) is mentioned as an imperial province involved in rebellion and its suppression, functioning as a geographic stage for Darius’ restoration of order.

In the Susa Foundation Inscriptions, Harauvatiš (Avestan: Harahvaitī) is mentioned as a source region for materials used in royal construction, integrated into the imperial supply network of Darius I.
In the Naqsh-e Rustam inscriptions, Harauvatiš (Harahvaitī) appears as one of the lands listed under the dominion of Darius I and Xerxes I.

Haoma is explicitly praised in Yasht 20, the short Haoma Yasht, and appears elsewhere in the Yashtic tradition as a divine ritual plant and drink associated with vitality, strength, and sacred offering.

Secondary Name: Yasna Haptanghaiti and Old Avestan Liturgy
Note: In the early liturgy, Ātar is a named and central sacred fire, ritually invoked and maintained, but not yet developed into a fully personified divine agent.
Ātar is explicitly invoked in the Younger Avestan corpus as sacred fire, called the son of Ahura Mazda and closely associated with Aša Vahišta, purity, and divine judgment.

The Gathas repeatedly invoke Ahura Mazda’s sacred fire as an agent of illumination, ritual power, and final judgment. Here Ātar is primarily fire itself as a divine force, not yet the fully personified yazata found in later Avestan texts.

Yima, son of Vivanghvant, is named in Yasna 32.8 among those whom Zarathustra criticizes, apparently for an act traditionally interpreted as introducing cattle flesh for human consumption. The passage is brief and much less celebratory than later accounts of Yima.

In the selected Yashts, Yima appears as the radiant king of good herds who once possessed royal glory. The detailed story of his enlarging the earth and constructing the Vara belongs specifically to Vendidad 2.

In the selected Yashts, Aži Dahāka is explicitly described as a three-mouthed, three-headed, six-eyed destructive monster opposed by Thraētaona; the later human tyrant Zahhāk belongs to subsequent Iranian epic development.
In the selected Yashts, Thraētaona is explicitly praised as the heroic conqueror of Aži Dahāka and a possessor or recipient of divine support and royal glory.
In Yasht 5, Arədvī Sūrā Anāhitā is explicitly praised as a powerful water divinity who grants fertility, health, victory, and prosperity to qualified worshippers and royal petitioners.

Secondary Name: Royal Inscriptions of Artaxerxes I and II
Note: In inscriptions of Artaxerxes II, Anāhitā is explicitly invoked together with Ahura Mazda and Mithra to protect the king and his building. This does not apply to the inscriptions of Artaxerxes I in the same bundled entry.
Yasht 14 is dedicated to Verethragna, the divine force of victory, who manifests in a sequence of powerful forms and grants strength, martial success, and overcoming power.

The Farvardin Yasht explicitly venerates the fravashi of Manuščiθra, the Avestan figure later known as Manūčehr. In later Iranian genealogy he belongs to the Pishdadian or pre-Kayanian line, not the Kayanian dynasty.
The Farvardin Yasht explicitly venerates the fravashi of Syāvaršan, the Avestan figure later known as Siyāvaš. The elaborate account of his unjust death belongs to later epic tradition.

The selected Yashts, especially the Zamyad and Farvardin Yashts, explicitly present Haosravah as a divinely favored Kayanian ruler associated with khvarenah, the defeat of hostile powers, and the veneration of his fravashi.
Vištāspa is explicitly named in the Gathas as an important supporter and patron of Zarathustra’s cause. The fully developed story of his conversion to the Good Religion belongs to later tradition.
The Younger Avesta explicitly names Kavi Vištāspa as a supporter of Zarathustra and venerates his fravashi; the detailed dramatic conversion narrative belongs to later Zoroastrian literature.

Zarathustra is explicitly named in the Gathas and frequently speaks in the first person, addressing Ahura Mazda, teaching, petitioning, and confronting opponents. His formal description as a chosen prophet is a traditional interpretation.

The Naqsh-e Rustam inscriptions call Darius and Xerxes “Achaemenid,” creating an indirect dynastic link to the eponymous ancestor Achaemenes. They do not name Achaemenes directly; Behistun supplies the explicit genealogy.
CMa and CMb explicitly name Cyrus and call him king and Achaemenid. The Old Persian inscriptions were probably added under Darius I, so the words may not have been commissioned by Cyrus himself.
Cyrus the Great was the father and royal predecessor of Cambyses II, who succeeded him as king and completed the conquest of Egypt.
In the Behistun Inscription, Darius I presents himself as the divinely sanctioned king chosen by Ahura Mazda who rightfully seized the throne and suppressed widespread rebellions to restore order.

In the Susa Foundation Inscriptions, Darius I is portrayed as a great builder-king who, by the favor of Ahura Mazda, constructs his palace at Susa using materials and labor drawn from across the empire.
In the Naqsh-e Rustam inscriptions, Darius I presents himself as the just, divinely favored “king of kings,” emphasizing his lineage, moral authority, and role as upholder of arta (truth and order).
The Persepolis Treasury archive begins in the final years of Darius I and preserves administrative records dated under his reign, including payments and transfers managed through the royal center.
In the Naqsh-e Rustam inscriptions, Xerxes I presents himself as the legitimate successor of Darius I, emphasizing his royal lineage, divine favor from Ahura Mazda, and continuity of just kingship.
A substantial portion of the Persepolis Treasury archive belongs to the reign of Xerxes I and documents payments, workers, officials, and palace administration under his government.
In XPa, Xerxes explicitly identifies himself as great king and states that, by the favor of Ahura Mazda, he built the Gate of All Nations at Persepolis.

Secondary Name: Royal Inscriptions of Artaxerxes I and II
Note: In the Royal Inscriptions of Artaxerxes II, Artaxerxes II presents himself as the legitimate great king of the Achaemenid line, ruling by the favor of Ahura Mazda and notably invoking not only Ahura Mazda but also Anahita and Mithra as divine protectors of his kingship.

Secondary Name: Yasna Haptanghaiti and Old Avestan Liturgy
Note: The Gathas and the Yasna Haptanghaiti are the two principal components of the Old Avestan corpus and were transmitted together within the received Yasna. They share language and ritual setting but neither cites the other as a separate work.
Ahura Mazda relates to Khshathra Vairya as the expression of ideal sovereignty, representing the rightful exercise of power in accordance with divine order.
Ahura Mazda relates to Haurvatat as the realization of completeness and well-being, embodying the perfected state of his creation.
Ahura Mazda relates to Ameretat as the principle of enduring life, ensuring the eternal continuation and preservation of his perfected order.

Secondary Name: Yasna Haptanghaiti and Old Avestan Liturgy
Note: Khshathra is explicitly invoked in the Yasna Haptanghaiti as desirable or good dominion, closely associated with Ahura Mazda, Aša, and Vohu Manah.

In the Gathas, Khshathra (proto–Khshathra Vairya) functions as the idealized form of power and sovereignty aligned with Asha—a dominion to be consciously chosen and realized through righteousness rather than force.
Khshathra Vairya is explicitly named in the Younger Avestan corpus among the Amesha Spentas as desirable dominion and divinely ordered power.
In the Gathas, Haurvatat represents wholeness, completeness, and spiritual well-being. It is regularly paired with Ameretat as a blessing associated with Ahura Mazda, Asha, and righteous action.
Haurvatat is explicitly named in the Younger Avestan corpus among the Amesha Spentas as wholeness or completeness; developed Zoroastrian tradition especially associates Haurvatat with water.
In the Gathas, Ameretat represents immortality or deathless life. Paired with Haurvatat, it describes the enduring life promised through alignment with Ahura Mazda’s truth and Good Mind.
Ameretat is explicitly named in the Younger Avestan corpus among the Amesha Spentas as immortality; developed Zoroastrian tradition especially associates Ameretat with plants and nourishment.

The selected Younger Avestan Yashts inherit Old Avestan concepts such as Ahura Mazda, asha, sacred speech, and Zarathustra’s authority while greatly expanding the individually praised divine and heroic world.

Primary Name: Yasna Haptanghaiti and Old Avestan Liturgy
Note: The selected Yashts continue Old Avestan patterns of invocation, praise, sacrifice, and devotion to Ahura Mazda, while directing full hymns to a broader body of individual yazatas and heroic figures.

The Vendidad belongs to the later Avestan priestly tradition and incorporates inherited Gathic formulas and prayers into purification and protective contexts; it does not cite “The Gathas” as a separately titled book.

Primary Name: Yasna Haptanghaiti and Old Avestan Liturgy
Note: The Yasna Haptanghaiti and the Vendidad belong to different layers and functions of the Avestan ritual tradition. They share Mazda-worship, sacred creation, ritual speech, and concern for maintaining ordered relations between worshippers and the divine world.

The selected Yashts and the Vendidad are distinct Younger Avestan corpora that share divine figures, heroic traditions, sacred geography, and cosmic opposition while serving different functions: hymnic praise and myth in the Yashts, and ritual-purity instruction in the Vendidad.

The Behistun Inscription explicitly names Achaemenes at the beginning of Darius’s genealogy as the ancestor from whom the Achaemenid line takes its name. The claim is central to Darius’s dynastic legitimation, although Achaemenes’s independent historicity remains uncertain.

CMa and CMb call Cyrus an “Achaemenid,” indirectly linking him to the eponymous ancestor Achaemenes. Because the inscriptions were probably added under Darius, this label also participates in later dynastic legitimation.
The Behistun Inscription explicitly names Cyrus as the father of Cambyses and places the preceding royal house within the family to which Darius claims to belong.

Cambyses is a major figure in the Behistun narrative: Darius identifies him as Cyrus’s son and predecessor, recounts the killing of Bardiya, his Egyptian campaign, his death, and the succession crisis exploited by Gaumata. The account is Darius’s partisan justification of his accession.

The surviving CMa and CMb inscriptions commemorate Cyrus but were probably carved during a second phase of work at Pasargadae under Darius I. Their connection to Darius is therefore one of likely commissioning and dynastic presentation rather than explicit self-reference.
The Persepolis Fortification Tablets are dated to 509–494 BCE, the thirteenth through twenty-eighth regnal years of Darius I, and document the administrative system operating from his royal center.

Xerxes I is the speaker and commissioning king of XPh. He presents his kingship as granted by Ahura Mazda, lists subject lands, and states that he destroyed a place where daiva were worshipped and established proper worship; the place and political context remain disputed.
Vendidad 1 explicitly names Harahvaitī as one of the good lands created by Ahura Mazda, corresponding to Old Persian Harauvatiš and the region conventionally called Arachosia.
Aži Sruvara is explicitly named in the Avestan heroic material preserved in the selected Yashts as the poisonous, horse- and man-devouring dragon slain by Kərəsāspa.

Vendidad 2 is the principal surviving Avestan narrative of Yima: Ahura Mazda asks him to preserve and enlarge the world and later commands him to construct the Vara that protects chosen humans, animals, and plants from a catastrophic winter.
Vendidad 1 explicitly refers to Aži Dahāka in connection with Varena, the land in which Thraētaona was born and from which the dragon-slayer tradition is recalled.
Vendidad 1 explicitly names Thraētaona as the hero born in Varena who smote Aži Dahāka; later chapters also invoke his fravashi in protective and healing contexts.

Zarathustra is the human interlocutor throughout the Vendidad. He repeatedly questions Ahura Mazda about lands, purity, pollution, ritual procedure, punishment, medicine, and protection against demonic forces.

The Vendidad explicitly uses āθravan as a designation for a Zoroastrian priest and distinguishes legitimate priestly qualification from false claims to the office, especially in its discussion of the unworthy priest.

Ātar, the fire of Ahura Mazda, is explicitly named throughout the Vendidad. The text regulates protection of fire from corpse pollution, refers to fire in ritual purification, and treats it as a sacred presence that must not be contaminated.

Vendidad 20 explicitly states that the primordial healer Thrita obtained a source of remedies from Khshathra Vairya, linking desirable dominion and its later association with metal to the origin of surgical healing.

Darius I was the father and royal predecessor of Xerxes I. Xerxes repeatedly grounds his legitimacy in descent from Darius and presents his building and imperial rule as a continuation of his father’s kingship.

Within the literary narrative of the Book of Esther, Esther becomes queen and consort of Ahasuerus, conventionally identified with Xerxes I. This is a scriptural-literary relationship and is not independently confirmed by Achaemenid records.
Thraētaona/Ferīdūn is the canonical conqueror of Aži Dahāka/Zahhāk. In the Avesta the conflict is dragon-slaying; in later Persian epic it becomes the overthrow and imprisonment of a tyrannical king.
In later Persian epic, Kāveh leads the public revolt against Zahhāk, rejects the tyrant’s declaration of legitimacy, and raises his leather apron as the banner of rebellion.
Ferīdūn and Kāveh are allied in the later epic overthrow of Zahhāk: Kāveh mobilizes resistance and brings popular support to Ferīdūn’s claim, while Ferīdūn defeats and binds the tyrant.

In later Iranian genealogy, Manūčehr is a descendant of Ferīdūn through Iraj. His accession and vengeance against the lines of Salm and Tur continue the dynastic consequences of Ferīdūn’s division of the world.
Siyāvaš is the father of Kai Khosrow. Kai Khosrow’s return, accession, and campaign against Afrāsiāb are framed in later epic as the vindication and avenging of his murdered father.
Rostam is the father of Sohrāb in the Persian epic tradition. Their fatal encounter turns on concealed identity: Rostam kills the young warrior before recognizing him as his son.

Goštāsp is the father and king of Esfandiyār in later Zoroastrian and epic tradition. Esfandiyār’s campaigns and final mission against Rostam are repeatedly shaped by his father’s commands and delayed promise of succession.

Zarathustra and Vištāspa are linked as religious teacher and royal patron. The Gathas name Vištāspa among Zarathustra’s supporters, while later tradition expands this into the king’s dramatic conversion and protection of the new religion.

Rostam and Esfandiyār are tragic adversaries in later Persian epic. Esfandiyār, compelled by Goštāsp to bind Rostam, is ultimately killed by Rostam with the specially prepared tamarisk arrow revealed through Sīmurgh’s aid.
The silver beaker is a specific inscribed object associated with Puzur-Sušinak/Kutik-Inshushinak and belongs within the broader corpus of royal and votive inscriptions attributed to that ruler.

Secondary Name: Linear Elamite Inscriptions from Susa (partially deciphered)
Note: The silver beaker is one artifact within the wider corpus of Linear Elamite inscriptions from Susa and related contexts. Its proposed reading therefore depends on the still-debated decipherment of that script.

The Fortification and Treasury tablets are successive, partly overlapping administrative archives from Persepolis. Together they document a shift in surviving records from regional commodity movements under Darius toward palace-centered disbursements, including silver payments, under Darius, Xerxes, and Artaxerxes I.
